Volume 04 · Chapter 09

Prediction and model validation

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v04-c08

By the endEvaluate models using splits that respect economic timing and information availability.

Evaluate the procedure that will actually be used

Capability: evaluate predictions using data splits and information sets that match the economic decision. Prerequisite: identification and confounding, the regression chapter and forecast losses and information. A forecast can be useful without identifying a causal effect; a causally credible estimate can still predict individual outcomes poorly. This chapter evaluates prediction, with original synthetic examples throughout.

A firm selects a demand model because its historical errors are small. Six months later, its budget misses badly. The discrepancy can arise even without a programming error: historical outcomes influenced the model choice, inputs may have been unavailable at forecast time, the validation period may differ from the operating environment, or the reported loss may measure the wrong consequence. A credible evaluation specifies the entire decision procedure before scoring its final performance.

Write a forecast as ŷt+h|t: a prediction of outcome Y at target date t+h, formed at origin t using information then available. The horizon h is elapsed time from origin to target. A record's reference period, release time and later revision time need not coincide. A December statistic released in February cannot be an input to a January forecast merely because its row is labeled December. For future outcomes measured over an interval, a training label may not become known until the interval and reporting delay have ended.

Declare the unit, population, forecast origin, horizon, available features, outcome definition, loss and updating rule. Forecasting next month's demand for existing stores differs from forecasting sales for a new store in a new region. A split that estimates one task may misrepresent the other. Record data vintages and availability as in the provenance chapter.

What an honest evaluation estimates

For an independent-observation setting, let T denote the training data and fT the complete fitted prediction rule, including its learned transformations. With a specified deployment distribution P for a new (X,Y), conditional prediction risk is

R(fT) = EP[L(Y, fT(X)) | T].

The rule is fixed conditional on T. If m test observations are drawn independently from that same distribution and are independent of everything used to construct the rule, then their average loss R̂test = m−1ΣL(Yi,fT(Xi)) satisfies E[R̂test | T] = R(fT) by linearity and the common conditional distribution. Independence among the test observations is not needed for this expectation identity if their marginals remain correct, but it matters for the usual variance and standard-error calculations. A distribution shift, selected test sample or adaptive reuse of test outcomes changes the argument.

This evaluates the particular trained rule. Averaging also over repeated training sets evaluates a learning procedure at that training size. Cross-validation generally trains on smaller subsets than the final fit, so its target is related but not identical. A chronological evaluation instead describes losses across its stated dates and forecasting protocol. It does not become an unbiased estimate of every future regime merely by being chronological.

Training loss uses observations that helped fit the rule. In nested least-squares models it can only improve when more columns are added, as already proved; future loss need not. Under squared loss, another useful identity separates the sources of error. At fixed x let μ(x) = E[Y | X=x], let a(x) = ET[fT(x)], and assume finite second moments and a new outcome independent of training conditional on x. Expand

Y − fT(x) = [Y − μ(x)] + [μ(x) − a(x)] + [a(x) − fT(x)].

The first and third terms have mean zero, and conditional independence makes their cross-product expectation zero. The other cross terms vanish for the same zero-mean reason. Consequently

ET,Y|x[(Y − fT(x))²] = Var(Y|x) + [μ(x) − a(x)]² + VarT(fT(x)).

The terms are conditional outcome noise, squared prediction bias and variability across training sets. A more flexible procedure may reduce approximation bias while becoming more sensitive to training data. This identity does not prove a universal tradeoff or that a particular flexible model is worse. The noise term is relative to the information X: adding useful available information can reduce it. The decomposition does not apply unchanged to a dependent future outcome or to absolute-error loss.

Choose a loss and a baseline before choosing a winner

For errors ei = yi − ŷi, mean absolute error is MAE = Σ|ei|/m, mean squared error is MSE = Σei²/m, and root mean squared error is RMSE = √MSE. MAE and RMSE have outcome units; MSE has squared units. On the same cases and weights, MSE and RMSE rank methods identically because the square root is increasing. MAE need not agree. A signed mean error diagnoses average direction, but positive and negative misses can cancel.

Expected squared loss targets a conditional mean, while expected absolute loss targets a conditional median; the earlier forecast chapter gives these decision-theoretic derivations. For positive finite costs cu and co, and finite conditional E[|Y| | X=x], let underprediction cost cu per unit and overprediction cost co. Then loss is cumax(y−a,0) + comax(a−y,0). Where the conditional distribution is continuous, differentiating expected loss gives (cu+co)F(a)−cu, so an optimal action is the cu/(cu+co) quantile. At atoms use the corresponding quantile inequality. A stock planner with unequal shortage and excess costs should not automatically optimize symmetric squared error.

Percentage measures need scrutiny. MAPE averages 100|ei/yi| and is undefined at y=0; near-zero denominators can dominate. A constant arbitrary offset changes the target rather than repairing the measure. For probabilities, use an appropriate proper score such as Brier or log loss, and assess calibration over relevant groups; accuracy after a threshold discards probability information. State weights explicitly: equal weight per firm, transaction or dollar of exposure defines different performance.

Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's author-hosted point-forecast accuracy chapter provides further discussion of forecast errors, unit-sensitive losses and percentage denominators. Our examples below use their own synthetic data, fixed comparison rules and explicit three-way selection/evaluation roles.

A baseline is a simple, genuinely available rule that the proposed method must justify improving upon. Options include a training-only mean, the latest available value, a seasonal value available at the same point in the cycle, or the current business rule. A baseline must receive the same information, score dates, loss and weights as its competitor. Comparing a complex method at one horizon with a baseline at another is not a valid performance comparison. A seasonal baseline needs a defined calendar and enough released history.

Worked example 1: two losses choose different methods

Four synthetic monthly demand outcomes are (10,20,20,20) units. Method A predicts (10,20,20,12); B predicts (7,17,17,17). Treat these as forecasts frozen before their respective outcomes, not fitted values chosen afterward.

Identical evaluation cases and equal weights
MethodErrors, unitsMAE, unitsMSE, units²RMSE, units
A0, 0, 0, 82164
B3, 3, 3, 3393

A has smaller total absolute error, 8 versus 12. B avoids the large miss and has smaller total squared error, 36 versus 64. Neither statement is an arithmetic contradiction. Under equal per-unit shortage costs with no overprediction here, A has the smaller realized cost. Under the specified quadratic penalty, B wins. Those four observations cannot establish which rule has lower population risk.

For a separate probability example, four binary outcomes are (1,0,1,0). A forecasts probability 0.5 every time; B forecasts (0.9,0.9,0.9,0.9). Their mean Brier scores are 0.25 and [0.01+0.81+0.01+0.81]/4 = 0.41. A threshold-only score would conceal how overconfident B is on the failures. Calibration and proper-score assessment require more than this tiny illustrative sample, and a good probability forecast is not automatically a profitable trading strategy after costs and constraints.

Separate fitting, selection and final evaluation

Training estimates coefficients and learns transformations. Validation compares candidate procedures, features, tuning parameters and other design choices. Test data evaluate the resulting locked procedure. These are information roles, not magic proportions: no universal 60/20/20 split can ensure enough data, credible timing or representative coverage. Reserve enough final cases to address the intended horizon and operating conditions.

A tuning parameter, or hyperparameter, controls a fitting procedure rather than being estimated by its ordinary fit; examples include model degree, a regularization strength or a rolling-window length. Once validation chooses it, a final model may be refitted on training plus validation observations before the test period, if that is the declared protocol. The test assesses that refitting procedure. Any preprocessing must be refitted consistently on the same permitted data.

Why does using the validation winner's score as its final assessment overstate performance? Suppose each fixed candidate j has an unbiased score R̂j for risk Rj. Pointwise, minjR̂j ≤ R̂k for every fixed k. Taking expectations and then the smallest Rk gives E[minjR̂j] ≤ minjRj. The selected candidate's true risk is at least that minimum, so its selected score is optimistic in this expectation comparison. Unbiased scores for fixed choices do not guarantee an unbiased score after choosing the smallest one.

For an exact original example, two candidates each have true risk 10. Each validation score independently equals 8 or 12 with probability 1/2. Each score is unbiased. The minimum is 12 only when both are 12, probability 1/4; otherwise it is 8. Thus its expected value is 9, while whichever method is selected still has true risk 10. The missing one unit is selection optimism. Real candidate errors are often dependent, and the numerical size of optimism differs; the inequality did not require independence.

Cawley and Talbot's original 2010 study of model-selection overfitting examines how optimizing a noisy selection criterion compromises evaluation. The two-candidate construction and inequality here expose the mechanism without relying on a particular learning algorithm.

Repeatedly examining a test result, revising the method and reporting the best revision turns that test into additional validation. Renaming it “untouched” afterward does not restore its role. Keep a new final sample, or explicitly report that evaluation is exploratory and seek later prospective evidence. Merely rerunning the same split with a new seed is not a fresh untouched sample.

Splits must respect time, groups and all learned steps

With exchangeable independent new units from a stable population, random disjoint partitions can approximate the intended deployment comparison. If many rows belong to the same household, firm or patient and the target is a new entity, put whole entities into separate folds. Otherwise a method may exploit entity-specific information that will be absent for a new entity. If the target instead concerns future records of known firms, a chronological within-firm design can be appropriate. Group separation alone does not enforce forecasting time; chronological separation alone does not test transfer to unseen firms.

In K-fold cross-validation, partition the development sample into K folds. For each fold fit the complete candidate procedure on the other folds and score the held-out observations; aggregate those losses. Every learned imputation rule, scaling constant, feature choice and tuning step must respect that fold's training data. When fold sizes differ, the pooled per-observation loss weights each fold by its observation count, rather than averaging fold means equally by accident. Folds with overlapping training samples do not supply independent estimates for a naive standard error across folds.

If cross-validation is itself choosing tuning parameters and also intended to evaluate the whole selection procedure, use an outer evaluation split and perform selection only within each outer training sample using inner splits. Refit the selected procedure on that outer training sample and score the untouched outer cases. This nested construction protects the outer evaluation role; it does not cure a wrong grouping rule, temporal leakage or distribution shift. A distinct final holdout can serve that role instead when the sample permits.

Leakage means information enters the procedure that its declared prediction task would not permit. Examples include a future outcome used as a feature, final revised values substituted for original releases, learning imputation constants from held-out data, choosing features against all labels before splitting, or putting duplicate records into both partitions. The violated contract matters even when a particular numerical result happens not to improve.

For a concrete preprocessing example, training feature values are 2 and 4; a training-only mean imputer fills a later missing value with 3. If a future test feature of 100 is also used to learn the imputation constant, the result becomes (2+4+100)/3 = 106/3. Under a fixed illustrative prediction formula 10+2x, the missing record's prediction changes from 16 to 242/3 ≈ 80.6667. This calculation proves unauthorized future information changed the prediction, not that it always improves the test score. If a task truly permits all unlabelled future inputs to be known together, that is a different, explicitly defined transductive task and needs a matching evaluation.

The developers' data-leakage guidance distinguishes fitting transformations on permitted training data from applying those learned transformations afterward. No scikit-learn installation is used here; the same information rule applies to spreadsheets and our standard-library programs.

Rolling origins and the availability of labels

A rolling-origin evaluation repeats the intended forecast in historical time. At each origin, reconstruct available inputs and labels, fit or update as declared, freeze the forecast, then score it after the target outcome becomes available. An expanding window retains all eligible past observations; a fixed-length rolling window retains a stated recent span. Window length is a model choice to select in development data. Neither window is guaranteed to handle a structural change well.

A gap between training and evaluation can be needed when labels span overlapping periods, information is released late, or adjacent observations share information forbidden by the deployment task. Determine the necessary exclusion from label end times, release dates and information flow. A fixed gap of one row is not a universal leakage remedy. Do not remove legitimate past information merely to make a dataset appear independent; specify which risk and operational information set the evaluation is meant to approximate.

Distinguish a forecast of several horizons issued once from successive forecasts that can learn newly released outcomes. At origin t, a four-month budget must use the information available at t for all four target months. A system that issues a new one-month forecast each month can update after each outcome arrives. Evaluating the second system and claiming the result for the first overstates the information available to the budget.

The author-hosted time-series cross-validation discussion introduces repeated origins and horizon-specific evaluation. The example below adds explicit release eligibility, development selection and a separate final period; its dates and numerical results are original.

Worked example 2: the validation winner loses later

Twelve synthetic monthly demand totals are (100,102,101,105,108,111,115,118,117,116,118,119), in units per month. For this model each total is known at the end of its own month, with no revisions. An origin just after month t closes can use months 1 through t. Initial training ends at month 4; targets 5–8 are validation, and targets 9–12 form the final evaluation. These boundaries, methods and loss are fixed in advance.

Compare three rules. Naive predicts the latest known value. Mean predicts the mean of the entire released history. Drift adds the average endpoint change per elapsed month to the latest value. With complete history through t, its one-step forecast is yt+(yt−y1)/(t−1). For h months ahead from the same origin, multiply that drift by h. This is an endpoint rule, not OLS on a time trend. It assumes no causal mechanism.

Validation: forecasts rebuilt at each preceding month-end
TargetActualNaiveMeanDriftDrift error
5108105102320/34/3
6111108516/51101
7115111209/2566/59/5
8118115106235/21/2

At origin 4 the endpoint drift is (105−100)/3 = 5/3, giving 105+5/3 = 320/3. Validation MSEs are 43/4 = 10.75 for naive, 35109/400 = 87.7725 for mean, and [(4/3)²+1²+(9/5)²+(1/2)²]/4 = 5641/3600 ≈ 1.566944 for drift. At the end of month 8 select drift. Ties, if any, would use the prespecified order naive, mean, drift. The selected procedure will continue updating each month with then-available labels.

Final one-step evaluation: method choice frozen after month 8; refitting rule unchanged
Origin → targetActualNaive forecastDrift forecastDrift error
8 → 9117118844/7−25/7
9 → 10116117953/8−25/8
10 → 111181161060/92/9
11 → 12119118599/5−4/5

The selected drift rule has final MSE 147393481/25401600 ≈ 5.802527 and RMSE ≈ 2.408844 units per month. Naive errors are (−1,−1,2,1), with MSE 7/4 = 1.75 and RMSE ≈ 1.322876. The expanding mean's final MSE is about 75.182913. The later data favor naive under the stated loss. Report that unfavorable comparison; do not silently replace the chosen rule and call its newly selected test score an untouched evaluation.

Using month 9's released outcome to form the month 10 forecast is allowed by this prespecified updating protocol. Using month 9 to revise the family of methods, loss or window length would be a new selection decision. The distinction is what is learned and when, not a prohibition on every future update. Four final months remain weak evidence about long-run relative performance, especially across changes in demand patterns.

If instead all four forecasts were issued once at origin 8, drift is 18/7 per month and predictions are 844/7, 862/7, 880/7 and 898/7. Against the same outcomes the errors are −25/7, −50/7, −54/7 and −65/7. Their MSE is 5133/98 ≈ 52.377551. It answers the fixed-budget question, not the repeatedly updated one-step question. The fixed-origin naive forecast stays 118 at every target and has MSE 3/2. Even the baseline's evaluation changes with the protocol.

Compare errors without inventing precision

Use the same target cases to compare two methods. A paired loss difference di = LA,i−LB,i measures which method did better on each case; its average is the difference in average loss. Under iid cases with finite variance, the standard error is sd/√m. Adding two separate mean-loss variance estimates ignores their covariance. Under serial, clustered or overlapping-horizon dependence, retain dependence in the uncertainty method; four chronological losses do not justify an iid t-test. Later econometrics develops appropriate dependence-aware inference.

Report baseline performance, loss units, horizon, number of scored cases, eligible and excluded populations, and conditions under which the result may transfer. Inspect performance across economically relevant groups without selecting only favorable slices. Separate explorations suggested by test failures from prespecified comparisons. A deployable financial strategy also requires feasible timing, transaction costs, constraints and risk assessment; a low prediction loss alone does not settle those questions.

Reproduce and challenge the information contract

Download the synthetic release-indexed inputs, exact Python benchmark and README. Run python3 v04-c09-validation.py. Fractions in the report give both exact and decimal representations. The code has no network dependency and does not modify inputs. It validates complete monthly keys, integer units, nonnegative demand and release dates, and refuses to select a method at month 8 if a validation outcome has not yet been released.

The computation separates history_as_of, which filters permitted observations, from forecast, which receives only that history and the target index. Actual target outcomes enter the later scoring function. If a label is delayed, drift uses the elapsed time from the latest released month to the target, not merely one row step. The complete rule needs at least two released observations. Its declared small-data bounds keep the example inspectable; it is not a production forecasting service.

Audit the information boundary by changing future labels. Changing only month 12's value must leave the validation winner and all forecasts through month 12 unchanged; only its realized loss changes. Changing month 9 can affect the allowed updates for months 10–12, but cannot alter the month 9 forecast or the method selected at month 8. Delaying month 8's release to month 9 must prevent selection at month 8. These checks expose look-ahead bugs more directly than simply comparing two runs of the same implementation.

Exercises

  1. Specify the forecast. On 1 March a lender predicts each existing borrower's default over March–May. A training loan's outcome window ends on 31 March and its label arrives on 15 April. State the unit, origin, horizon/outcome window, permitted training labels and a suitable chronological evaluation. Would random row splitting test performance on entirely new borrowers if borrowers have repeated records?
  2. Loss and asymmetric cost. Recompute example 1's MAE/MSE/RMSE. Then let shortage cost be 9 USD per unit and excess-stock cost be 1 USD per unit. For a predictive demand distribution putting probability 0.8 on 10 units and 0.2 on 20, compare actions 10, 12 and 20 by expected cost and identify an optimal action. Explain why a conditional-mean forecast need not be optimal for this decision.
  3. Selection optimism. Enumerate the four equally likely two-candidate validation-score pairs in the 8/12 example. Find the mean selected score and compare it with the selected method's true risk. Generalize the pointwise inequality to any finite number of unbiased candidate scores. Does it require their independence?
  4. Reconstruct the chronological comparison. Derive the month 7 drift forecast from its actual available history, then calculate all validation drift errors and MSE. Calculate naive final MSE and the difference between selected drift and naive final MSE. State what can and cannot be inferred from that difference.
  5. Frozen or updating? Derive origin-8 drift forecasts for all four final targets and their MSE. Recompute the fixed-origin naive MSE. Explain why using month 9's outcome in month 10's one-step forecast can be legitimate while using it for a forecast originally issued at origin 8 is not. How does a delayed month-9 release affect the information set at origin 9?
  6. Preprocessing and leakage audit. Reconstruct the 2,4,100 imputation example. Identify the leaked information and why the changed prediction does not prove a lower test loss. A researcher selects the ten predictors most correlated with all observed outcomes, then cross-validates a regression on those ten predictors. Specify the repair, including the final evaluation role if the feature count is also selected.
  7. Weighting and paired uncertainty. Two evaluation folds have sizes 2 and 8 and MSEs 1 and 9. Compute their pooled per-observation MSE and their unweighted mean fold MSE. For a separate iid four-case comparison, A's squared losses are (0,0,0,64) and B's are (9,9,9,9). Compute the paired mean difference, its sample variance and standard error. Explain why substituting the four chronological targets from example 2 would not automatically justify the iid standard-error interpretation.
  8. Challenge a performance claim. Run the offline laboratory and one of its future-label/release mutations. A manager wants to switch to naive after seeing the final losses and advertise 1.75 as independently validated performance of the entire search. Write a corrected report and a plan for the next evaluation. Include target, loss, information set, updating rule, candidate selection, baseline and a meaningful remaining uncertainty.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. The unit is an existing borrower or a precisely defined loan–borrower exposure, with duplicate exposures and aggregation declared. The origin is 1 March; the target is default during the three-month March–May window, not just the May-end status without a definition. Only labels whose outcome windows have ended and whose releases have arrived by the origin may train the rule. The label released 15 April is unavailable on 1 March even if the loan record starts earlier. An evaluation reconstructs successive past 1-March-like origins, fits on then-available data, freezes predictions and scores after follow-up matures. Respect overlapping outcome windows and release delays when defining development/evaluation separation. Repeated borrower rows split randomly can place the same entity on both sides; that does not assess generalization to wholly new borrowers. A new-borrower target requires borrower-level separation plus the appropriate timing. A complete answer states feature availability and does not equate row date with label availability.
  2. A's errors (0,0,0,8) give MAE 2, MSE 16, RMSE 4; B's (3,3,3,3) give 3, 9, 3. The asymmetric cost targets a 9/(9+1)=0.9 quantile. Action 10 costs 0.8(0)+0.2(9×10)=18 USD. Action 12 costs 0.8(1×2)+0.2(9×8)=16 USD. Action 20 costs 0.8(1×10)+0.2(0)=8 USD. For any a between 10 and 20, expected cost is 0.8(a−10)+1.8(20−a)=28−a, decreasing toward 20; below 10 it decreases as a rises, and above 20 it increases. Thus 20 is optimal. The mean is 12, optimal for squared prediction loss but not for this shortage/excess decision.
  3. The score pairs are (8,8), (8,12), (12,8), (12,12), with selected scores 8,8,8,12. Their average is 9. Each candidate's true risk is 10, so selection does not change that true risk but lowers the expected reported score by 1. For any fixed k, minjR̂j≤R̂k; taking expectations gives E[min R̂]≤Rk when each score is unbiased. Minimizing the right-hand side gives E[min R̂]≤min R. Also Rselected≥min R for every selection, so the expected selected score cannot exceed the expected selected true risk under these premises. Independence is needed for the four equally likely pairs in the numerical construction, not for the general inequality. Finite expectations and fixed candidate-risk definitions matter.
  4. At origin 6, history ends at y6=111 and begins at y1=100; five elapsed months give drift 11/5. Month 7 forecast is 111+11/5=566/5=113.2, hence error 115−113.2=9/5. The complete validation errors are 4/3,1,9/5,1/2, giving MSE 5641/3600≈1.566944. Naive final errors −1,−1,2,1 give MSE 7/4. The selected drift's final MSE minus naive's is 102940681/25401600≈4.052527 in squared monthly-demand units. These later constructed cases favor naive under this loss/protocol. They neither invalidate the recorded validation choice nor prove a universal future advantage; the comparison has only four outcomes and may reflect changed patterns. The final score cannot be reused as an untouched estimate of a newly chosen winner.
  5. Origin-8 drift is (118−100)/(8−1)=18/7. At horizons 1–4, predictions 118+h(18/7) equal 844/7,862/7,880/7,898/7. Errors against 117,116,118,119 are −25/7,−50/7,−54/7,−65/7, with MSE(625+2500+2916+4225)/(49×4)=5133/98≈52.377551. Fixed-origin naive predicts 118 four times; errors −1,−2,0,1 give MSE 6/4=3/2. In an updating task, y9 is permitted after release and before forecasting target10. It was unavailable at origin8 and cannot enter forecasts issued then. If month9 is released only at end10, origin9 must omit it. With all other original releases unchanged, the latest available value is118 from month8, and the drift target10 forecast is118+2(18/7)=862/7. At origin10, newly released months9 and10 can both enter the declared updating rule.
  6. The permitted imputation constant is (2+4)/2=3, giving10+2×3=16. Including the future100 yields106/3 and forecast10+2(106/3)=242/3. A held-out feature distribution influenced a fitted transformation despite the declared sequential task. The actual missing record's outcome is unspecified, so no claim about the direction of its loss change follows. For feature selection, each fold must select predictors using only its own training labels and then fit/apply the resulting model to that fold's held-out cases. If feature count is also tuned, select it with inner development splits and evaluate the full selection process on untouched outer folds or a separate final test. Splitting after selecting against all labels leaks outcome information even if subsequent regression code is correct.
  7. Fold sums of squared errors are2×1=2 and8×9=72; pooled MSE 74/10=7.4. The unweighted fold average is(1+9)/2=5 and gives each fold equal weight despite their unequal case counts. For the separate paired comparison d=(−9,−9,−9,55); its mean is 7. Deviations are−16,−16,−16,48, whose squares sum 3072. Sample variance is 3072/3=1024, and iid standard error is√(1024/4)=16. A's mean loss16 minus B's9 also gives 7. Pairing retains covariance induced by scoring the same cases. Time-ordered losses may be serially dependent, share estimation histories or span overlapping horizons; dividing by√4 alone does not address these dependencies. Even in the iid illustration, four cases provide a fragile basis for distributional inference.
  8. A satisfactory report preserves the exact original selection rule, its validation score and the drift final score ≈ 5.802527 versus naive 1.75. Switching after examining the final period is a new development decision. Describe 1.75 as naive's observed loss on the four reported synthetic months, not an untouched estimate of the whole adaptive search. Demonstrate that a future-label edit leaves earlier forecasts/selection unchanged, or that a release delay removes an unavailable input or prevents premature selection. Predeclare the new method and any updating/window rules, collect a subsequent evaluation period with mature labels, retain the same economic loss and baseline, and state the target population/horizon and information-time rule. Report uncertainty from limited periods and potential demand changes. Equivalent plans receive full credit if they preserve evaluation independence appropriate to their task and avoid causal or guaranteed-profit claims.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back: explain why training, validation and test are different information roles; derive the two-candidate optimism example; then explain exactly which past test labels an updating forecast may use. Use the origin-8 and origin-9 calculations to distinguish legitimate refitting from retrospective selection.

Delayed check: after one week, reconstruct the month-5 and month-9 drift forecasts without the table. Explain how a late release changes eligible history. Give one task requiring group separation, one requiring chronological separation, and one requiring both. Recalculate the asymmetric-loss optimal action and explain why it differs from the mean.

Delayed-check answer

The forecasts are 105+(105−100)/3=320/3 and 118+(118−100)/7=844/7. Include a record only when its reference period and release are no later than the origin. New entities require group separation; later outcomes for known entities require temporal separation; future outcomes for new entities require both. With probabilities 0.8/0.2 and shortage/excess costs 9/1, the 0.9 quantile is 20, whereas the mean is 12. The former minimizes the stated operational loss.

Next: time-series and panel data basics makes the calendar, dependence, aggregation and population questions more explicit. Advanced model classes, regularization and formal forecast-comparison inference are developed later; this chapter establishes the evaluation contract they must satisfy.

Sources and further study

  • Rob J Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos — Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition, 5.8 Evaluating point forecast accuracy — Further study of forecast versus fitted errors, MAE/RMSE units and percentage-denominator limitations. The chapter develops original examples and an explicit separate validation role.
  • Hyndman and Athanasopoulos — Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition, 5.10 Time series cross-validation — Further study of rolling origins and horizon-specific forecast evaluation. The original lab adds explicit releases, candidate selection and fixed-origin versus updating protocols.
  • scikit-learn developers — Common pitfalls: Data leakage — Training-only learning of preprocessing transformations and applying them consistently on held-out data. Principle is used in an original small stdlib teaching case, without a scikit-learn dependency.
  • Gavin C. Cawley and Nicola L. C. Talbot (2010), On Over-fitting in Model Selection and Subsequent Selection Bias in Performance Evaluation — Original research route on optimizing noisy model-selection criteria and evaluation bias. Chapter supplies its own finite two-candidate example and expectation inequality.
